t: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones — Interval DP with a Twist
o:
We must repeatedly merge exactly $k$ consecutive piles into one, paying the sum of their stones each time, until (possibly) one pile remains. This is an interval DP problem: the cost of merging range [i, j] depends on how we split it into subranges. First, feasibility: each merge reduces pile count by k-1, so we can end with 1 pile iff (n-1) % (k-1) == 0; otherwise return -1 immediately.

**Example 1** ([3,2,4,1], k=2): merge [3,2]→5, merge [4,1]→5, merge [5,5]→10; total 20. **Example 2** ([3,2,4,1], k=3): n=4, (4-1)%(3-1)=1≠0, impossible → -1. **Example 3** ([3,5,1,2,6], k=3): merge [5,1,2]→8 leaving [3,8,6], then merge all three for 17; total 25.

With n ≤ 30, an O(n³·k)-ish DP is easily fast enough.
k: Feasibility check first: merging is possible iff (n - 1) % (k - 1) == 0.
Interval DP state dp[i][j][m] = min cost to merge stones[i..j] into exactly m piles; final answer is dp[0][n-1][1].

When splitting [i..j] into left/right parts, only the right part's pile count matters mod (k-1), because any subrange of length L must reduce to ((L-1) % (k-1)) + 1 piles — this collapses the third dimension of transitions.

a.i: Define f(i, j, m) = minimum cost to combine stones[i..j] into exactly m piles. Base case: a single element forms 1 pile at cost 0. To build m piles from [i..j], split after some index mid: the left part [i..mid] becomes m-1 piles and the right part [mid+1..j] becomes 1 pile. A key fact: any contiguous segment of length L can only ever be reduced to ((L-1) % (k-1)) + 1 piles, so when the right part has exactly k piles we pay prefix[j+1]-prefix[i] to fuse everything into one. Memoization over O(n²·k) states with O(n) splits gives roughly O(n³·k).
s: Compute prefix sums so any range sum is O(1).
Memoized function f(i, j, m): if i == j return 0 iff m == 1 else infinity.
For each split point mid from i to j-1 step (k-1), try f(i, mid, m-1) + f(mid+1, j, 1); if m == 1, additionally add the range sum once the whole segment reduces to k piles.
a.t: O(n^3 · k) time — O(n² · k) states, each trying up to n/k split points; trivially fast for n ≤ 30.
a.sp: O(n² · k) for the memo table plus recursion stack up to O(n).

a.i: Same recurrence computed iteratively by increasing interval length. dp[i][j][m] is the min cost to reduce stones[i..j] to m piles. Transitions mirror the top-down version: split into a left part with m-1 piles and a right part with 1 pile, and when m == 1, take the best cost of reducing [i..j] to k piles plus the total range sum. Filling by increasing length guarantees all needed subintervals are ready.
s: Initialize dp[i][i][1] = 0 and everything else to infinity.
Iterate lengths from 2 to n; for each [i, j], iterate m from 2 to k, then handle m == 1 via dp[i][j][k] + rangeSum(i, j).
Split points step by k-1 since intermediate pile counts are constrained mod (k-1).
a.t: O(n^3 · k) time — triple loop over intervals, splits, and pile counts.
a.sp: O(n² · k) for the dp table; no recursion overhead.

w: In an interview, lead with the feasibility check ((n-1) % (k-1) == 0), then present the memoized version — it's easier to reason about — and mention the bottom-up variant as an optimization. Common pitfalls: forgetting the -1 case entirely; stepping split points by 1 instead of k-1 (still correct but slower and conceptually muddier); mishandling the m==1 transition where you must first reduce to k piles and then pay the full range sum; and integer overflow in Java/C++ without long sums (max total ≈ 30·100 per merge, ~900 merges worst case — safe with long). Edge cases: n == 1 returns 0; k > n returns -1 unless n == 1. Follow-ups: prove why every segment of length L reduces to exactly ((L-1) % (k-1)) + 1 piles, or generalize to merging any k consecutive piles chosen greedily (Huffman-like, which fails here because contiguity constrains choices).
